reasoning: Patient is 4 days old (0.1 months) — neonatal period carries inherently high risk; sepsis, NEC, and hemorrhagic disease present atypically and deteriorate rapidly

Chief complaint: blood in diaper — differential includes physiologic bleeding (uric acid crystals, vaginal bleeding from maternal hormone withdrawal), but also hemorrhagic disease of newborn (vitamin K deficiency), NEC, urinary tract pathology, or early infection with hematuria
No vital signs recorded — this is itself a RED FLAG in a neonate; inability to obtain or document vitals in a 4-day-old with bleeding warrants immediate assessment and uptriage

Patient appears well (nursing, alert, sleeping) — reassuring but does NOT exclude serious pathology; neonatal sepsis and life-threatening conditions often present with minimal early signs; clinical appearance is an unreliable sole discriminator in infants <7 days
Birth weight appropriate (7 lb 2 oz) — reduces concern for prematurity-related complications but does not eliminate risk
Age <7 days places patient in highest-risk window for early-onset sepsis, hemorrhagic disease, and metabolic derangements

Per ESI framework: patient has not yet received vital signs or physician evaluation — meets resource threshold (labs, imaging, pediatric assessment required); combined with age-specific danger (neonatal period) and bleeding complaint, escalates beyond level 3
When vital signs cannot be obtained or documented in a neonate with an acute complaint (bleeding), default to higher acuity pending evaluation

ESI Decision Point D (high-risk situation): age <7 days + bleeding + no vitals documented = meets criteria for level 2 (high-risk situation, should not wait for full workup before physician evaluation)
red_flags: Neonatal age (4 days) — highest-risk window for overwhelming sepsis, NEC, hemorrhagic disease, and metabolic crises
Bleeding reported (blood on diaper) — unexplained bleeding in neonate until proven benign
Vital signs NOT RECORDED at triage — inability to document baseline in a sick-appearing or acutely symptomatic neonate is a safety concern
No prior medical record — no baseline, no known risk factors, no prior evaluation to compare
Deceptively well appearance — neonatal sepsis and serious illness may present with minimal signs; somnolence is atypical and could represent early compensation
Nursing well may falsely reassure; feeding tolerance does not exclude systemic infection in first week of life
